stemBlocks.value: A rectangular door is 2.40 m high and 0.90 m wide. A wooden brace is fixed from one corner to the opposite corner. a) Calculate the required length of the brace, giving your answer to the nearest centimetre. b) A carpenter has a piece of timber 2.55 m long. Decide whether it is long enough and justify your answer numerically.
Think first: The brace is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle whose legs are the height and width of the door.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p168-q01 from workbook page 168.

contentBlocks.value: The height and width meet at a corner at 90°, and the brace joins the opposite corners
Result: legs 2.40 m and 0.90 m, hypotenuse = brace
Result: brace = 2.56 m to the nearest centimetre

solutionSteps.instruction: Compare the timber with the required length.
State the decision with the shortfall.

contentBlocks.value: Result: too short by about 1.3 cm

strategyBlocks.value: Apply Pythagoras to the 2.40 m and 0.90 m sides to get the diagonal, then compare that exact value with 2.55 m.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) The brace must be 2.56 m (to the nearest centimetre)  (b) No — the timber is 2.55 m but 2.5632 m is needed, so it falls short by about 0.013 m, roughly 1.3 cm

whyThisWorks.value: The two sides of a rectangle meet at a right angle, so the diagonal is always the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle and Pythagoras applies directly. In part b the comparison must be made against the unrounded value: rounding to 2.56 m first still gives the right decision here, but rounding before comparing is the habit that produces wrong answers in borderline cases.

commonErrors.misconception: Adding 2.40 and 0.90 instead of squaring, adding and square-rooting.
